title: The Rise of AI in Job Postings
author: Ben Perry

dom.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report documents rising and uneven employer demand for AI-related roles, especially in technology, but does not address legal workflows, bounded-task productivity, verification, lawyer replacement, or competence risks. Its job-posting evidence therefore cannot establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: The resulting data provides insight into how common AI is within job listings today, though how commonly depends a lot on role, function, and company size.
From the start of 2024 through Q2 2026, we see a rapid increase in AI in job titles for technical roles.

kp.k: Analysis covers over 200,000 postings through Q2 2026
kp.d: The report analyses over 200,000 qualifying job postings and their descriptions from the start of 2021 through Q2 2026. It defines an AI job broadly as any posting containing a relevant reference to AI, artificial intelligence, or similar terms in either the title or description; therefore, its measures capture textual references to AI rather than demonstrated AI use or task substitution.
qs: This report is based on over 200,000 qualifying job postings and corresponding job descriptions from the start of 2021 through Q2 of 2026.
AI jobs here refer to jobs with any relevant reference to AI, artificial intelligence, or similar terms in either the job description or the job title itself.
The resulting data provides insight into how common AI is within job listings today, though how commonly depends a lot on role, function, and company size.

kp.k: AI entered technical job titles rapidly after 2024
kp.d: The report finds that AI was rare in job titles until the start of 2024, more than a year after ChatGPT's public launch. From then through Q2 2026, AI terminology increased rapidly in technical titles but only modestly in business-function titles. Examples include AI Engineer, AI Infrastructure Engineer, AI Product Manager, and AI Solutions Specialist.
qs: Job titles with AI in the name were rare until 2024.
From the start of 2024 through Q2 2026, we see a rapid increase in AI in job titles for technical roles.
The appearance of AI in a job title was rare until the start of 2024, more than a full year after ChatGPT launched publicly.
Since then, AI has become considerably more common in tech roles while growing modestly in business functions.

AI Engineer, AI Infrastructure Engineer, AI Product Manager, and AI Solutions Specialist are examples of job titles that now appear with some frequency, many of which represent roles at leading AI companies.

kp.k: Most job titles still omit AI
kp.d: Despite the emergence of specialised AI roles, the report finds that most postings do not put AI in the title. Business roles in particular rarely have AI-labelled titles, even when their descriptions include AI-related requirements.
qs: Though business roles rarely feature AI as part of their title, AI is still incorporated into their list of job requirements.
Despite the recent emergence of AI-specific technical roles, most postings leave AI out of the job title.

kp.k: AI appears frequently in business job requirements
kp.d: For jobs with 2026 hire dates, the report says approximately one-third of business-role descriptions mention AI, compared with more than half of technical-role descriptions. This indicates that AI-related expectations extend beyond explicitly AI-labelled positions, although the source does not specify the content or depth of those requirements.
qs: AI appears in roughly one-third of business job posting descriptions with 2026 hired dates.
While that frequency is still well below the rate for tech roles, which is above 50%, it still represents a healthy fraction of all hired jobs.

kp.k: Engineering and data postings mention AI most often
kp.d: Based on postings dating from the start of 2025, the report finds substantial variation by job category. Engineering and Data roles referenced AI in their descriptions about half the time over the following year-plus. It states that business functions generally did not reach the same rate as technical roles, while identifying Legal as an exception to that generalisation without supplying a numerical legal-specific rate in the text.
qs: Whether a job references AI in its description varies considerably based on the category of job.
The chart below depicts the fraction of jobs with AI in the description dating back to the start of 2025.
Engineering or Data roles have referenced AI about half the time over the last year-plus.
Other business functions (except for Legal) don't have a significant number of roles that call out AI in their job descriptions at the same rate compared to tech roles.

kp.k: Smaller companies mention AI more than larger organisations
kp.d: The report finds that smaller companies explicitly include AI in job descriptions substantially more often than larger organisations. The author offers startup concentration and AI-focused venture funding as one possible interpretation, rather than presenting it as a demonstrated causal explanation.
qs: Smaller companies write AI into their postings more often than larger organizations.
Interestingly, smaller companies are more likely to include AI in their job descriptions by a significant margin.
While enterprises more often make the news with public declarations about the future of AI in the workplace, early stage startups explicitly tie their role responsibilities to AI more often.
One potential interpretation for this is that many new startups, and much of startup funding , remains focused on AI.

kp.k: AI mentions show no significant AMER-EMEA difference
kp.d: The report finds no significant regional discrepancy between AMER and EMEA in the share of job descriptions mentioning AI. On this measure, neither region appears to be incorporating AI into posted roles more than the other.
qs: Meanwhile, there does not appear to be a significant discrepancy in the share of descriptions mentioning AI across global regions, namely AMER and EMEA.
Neither region appears to be embracing AI in their posted roles more than the other.

kp.k: Technical AI roles require more proactive candidate sourcing
kp.d: For technical functions, jobs explicitly naming AI in their titles were less likely than other technical roles to be filled through inbound or referral applications and more likely to be filled through agencies and sourcing. The author interprets this pattern as suggesting that employers must identify AI candidates more proactively. Business functions were excluded from this comparison because AI rarely appears in their titles.
qs: Teams fill the top of the hiring funnel differently for AI roles than for non-AI roles.
Because AI so rarely appears in job titles for business functions, the following data covers technical functions only.
Tech jobs explicitly including AI in their titles are less likely to be filled from inbound or referral applications.
Instead, those hires come more often through agencies and sourcing.
This suggests that teams hiring for AI roles have to be more proactive in identifying AI candidates than for other tech roles.

kp.k: AI requirements are spreading unevenly across employment
kp.d: The report concludes that AI references are becoming widespread but remain uneven by role, function, and organisation size. Its claim that AI will probably become necessary for engineers, legal workers, and product managers is a forward-looking prediction, not a finding directly established by the posting-frequency analysis.
qs: The spread of AI in job descriptions is well underway, but it's still uneven.
Smaller organizations seem to be embracing AI more widely across listed jobs, and tech functions reference it more than business functions.
Regardless, whether you work as an engineer, in legal, or product management, there is a strong likelihood that AI will be a necessary component of your role going forward.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ben Perry reports that AI references are becoming more common in recruitment, particularly for technical roles and smaller companies, and predicts that AI will become a necessary component of work across functions, including legal.
pts.d: In this cross-domain hiring report, Perry claims that AI in job titles was rare until early 2024, then increased rapidly for technical roles while growing modestly in business functions. Most postings nevertheless omit AI from their titles. Among postings with 2026 hired dates, roughly one-third of business job descriptions and more than half of technical job descriptions mention AI. Engineering and Data descriptions have referenced AI about half the time since the start of 2025; Perry identifies Legal as an exception to the otherwise lower prevalence in business functions, without supplying a numerical legal-specific rate in the provided text. Smaller companies mention AI substantially more often than larger organizations. Perry offers the AI focus of new startups and startup funding as one possible explanation, not an established cause. He reports no significant difference between AMER and EMEA in the share of descriptions mentioning AI. For technical jobs explicitly naming AI in their titles, hires come less often from inbound or referral applications and more often from agencies and sourcing; he interprets this as suggesting a need for more proactive candidate identification. His concluding prediction concerns future role requirements, not demonstrated legal-service productivity, job displacement, or legal-market restructuring.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Perry bases the descriptive findings on more than 200,000 qualifying job postings and descriptions; the future-role prediction and explanations of hiring patterns are interpretations of those observations.
pts.d: The report defines AI jobs broadly through relevant AI references in either titles or descriptions, rather than through demonstrated AI use or exclusively AI-specialist responsibilities. It compares mentions by function, company size, region, and time, and compares hiring channels for technical AI-titled roles against other technical roles. The supplied text references charts but does not provide their numerical contents, subgroup counts, or statistical tests. Consequently, the legal-function exception, company-size difference, regional comparison, and hiring-channel differences can be preserved qualitatively but not assigned additional numerical magnitudes. Perry's suggested startup explanation and inference that AI hiring requires greater proactivity are explicitly interpretive. No separate forecast model or direct measurement of future workplace requirements is offered for his concluding prediction.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report covers early 2021 through Q2 2026, with narrower periods and samples for individual findings; its future prediction has no specified deadline.
pts.d: Published July 9, 2026, the report dates the acceleration in AI-titled technical postings to early 2024, more than a year after ChatGPT's public launch. The roughly one-third business-description and above-50% technical-description figures concern postings with 2026 hired dates. The function-level description comparison begins in early 2025. The hiring-channel analysis is restricted to technical functions because AI-titled business roles are rare. The regional comparison specifically concerns AMER and EMEA. Perry qualifies the overall trend as uneven across organization sizes and functions, and recognizes variation by role, seniority, geography, and industry. His prediction that AI will become necessary in roles is probabilistic and open-ended.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified effects concern job candidates, employees, and recruiting teams across technical and business functions, with Legal specifically included in the discussion of AI-related role expectations.
pts.d: Engineering and Data roles have especially frequent AI references, and AI-specific technical titles include AI Engineer, AI Infrastructure Engineer, AI Product Manager, and AI Solutions Specialist, many at leading AI companies. Business-role candidates may encounter AI requirements even where titles do not mention AI; Legal is singled out as an exception to the generally lower business-function prevalence. Early-stage startups tie responsibilities to AI more often than larger organizations. Recruiting teams filling AI-titled technical jobs rely more on agencies and active sourcing, while candidates are less often hired through inbound or referral applications. The prediction extends to engineers, legal workers, and product managers. The report does not distinguish law firms from in-house legal departments or identify effects on legal clients, fees, access to justice, or particular legal staffing structures.
